summary: Defines the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER) for ASN.1, a human-readable text encoding for values of any ASN.1 data type. This makes it easier to display and write values than with the binary encodings commonly used. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Computers often store data in a hard-to-read binary code. This provides a way to write the same information as readable text, like turning a secret code into plain words.

questions: how are asn.1 values written as text
subtitle: A readable text form for any ASN.1 value, built for describing LDAP directory data.

tldr.problem: ASN.1 values are normally sent in binary encodings that people cannot read, and LDAP directories needed a text form for their data types.
tldr.mechanism: GSER defines a UTF-8 text encoding for every ASN.1 type, based on ASN.1 value notation, with a rule for each type such as strings, integers, booleans, sequences and choices.
tldr.outcome: Referencing GSER is enough to define a human-readable encoding for a type. It is not canonical, so it must not be used where the original binary encoding has to be recovered. RFC 4792 updates it.

today: RFC 3641 is a Proposed Standard that is updated by RFC 4792. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why a String Encoding for ASN.1
sections.content:
RFC 3641 defines the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER). They produce a human-readable UTF-8 character string for a value of any ASN.1 type. An ASN.1 value is an abstract idea, independent of any encoding. The Basic Encoding Rules (BER) are just one way to write it down, and GSER is another.

GSER is based on ASN.1 value notation, changed so it works as a transfer syntax and so it fits older ad-hoc string encodings used for LDAP directory data types. It is mainly meant for defining the LDAP-specific encoding of new attribute syntaxes and assertion syntaxes, but the RFC says it could be used anywhere a readable rendering of ASN.1 values would help.

Referencing GSER is sufficient to define a text encoding for a type. Other specifications may add their own ABNF as a convenience, but they SHOULD say that the GSER encoding wins if the two disagree. Equivalent ABNF for the types commonly seen in LDAP is in RFC 3642.
sections.eli5: Imagine a toy that only understands beeps. GSER is a way to write what the beeps mean in words anyone can read.

sections.title: Strings and Type References
sections.content:
Tags and constraints on a type do not appear in GSER output. A tagged or constrained type is encoded as the plain type underneath, and a named or parameterized type is encoded according to its definition.

Every restricted character string type is written the same way: the contents as UTF-8 between double quotes. Any double quote inside the string is escaped by repeating it. This covers NumericString, PrintableString, IA5String, UTF8String, BMPString, UniversalString and the other restricted string types. GeneralizedTime, UTCTime and ObjectDescriptor values are also written as quoted strings.

Some ASN.1 types are a CHOICE between several string types where the choice carries no meaning. A specification can declare such a type a ChoiceOfStrings type. The alternatives must all be different restricted string types, and either none or all of them must carry the same constraint. This RFC declares every use of DirectoryString to be one, so its value is written as a plain quoted string.
sections.eli5: All the different kinds of text in the old format get written the same way: in quotation marks. If you want a quote mark inside, you write it twice.

sections.title: Simple Values
sections.content:
Each basic ASN.1 type gets its own small rule. A BOOLEAN is TRUE or FALSE, and NULL is written NULL. An INTEGER is a decimal number, or an identifier if the type has a named number list. An ENUMERATED value is one of the listed identifiers.

An OCTET STRING is written as pairs of hexadecimal digits between single quotes followed by H. A BIT STRING can be written as binary digits followed by B, as hex followed by H when the bit count is a multiple of four, or as a list of named bits in braces.

An OBJECT IDENTIFIER is dotted decimal or an object descriptor name, but the RFC warns that a descriptor name is potentially ambiguous and should be used with care. A REAL value is 0 when zero, otherwise PLUS-INFINITY, MINUS-INFINITY, a base 10 number, or a sequence form.
sections.eli5: Yes or no is written TRUE or FALSE, numbers are written as numbers, and raw bytes are written as pairs of letters and digits.

sections.title: Choices, Sequences and Sets
sections.content:
A CHOICE value is written as the chosen alternative's identifier, a colon and the value, for example identifier:Value. A ChoiceOfStrings value may instead be a plain quoted string. For a DirectoryString, a reader that cares about the internal structure assumes the printableString alternative if the characters are all legal in a PrintableString, and the uTF8String alternative otherwise. The identified form may be used to select a different alternative. Implementations that ignore the structure MUST still be able to parse the identified form.

A SEQUENCE is a brace-enclosed, comma-separated list of the components present, each preceded by its identifier, in the order of the type definition. A SET is written exactly the same way, which is a deliberate departure from ASN.1 value notation, where set components can come in any order. A SEQUENCE OF or SET OF is a brace-enclosed list of values.

Because types are sometimes extended later, an implementation SHOULD be able to skip a component whose identifier it does not recognise, assuming the sender uses a newer definition.
sections.eli5: A bag of labeled things is written as a list in curly brackets, each item with its label in front. If you see a label you do not know, you just skip that item.

sections.title: Variant Encodings and the Transfer Syntax
sections.content:
A few named complex types have special string encodings that are always used instead of the general rules. A distinguished name (an RDNSequence) is written as its string form from RFC 2253, then quoted like a UTF8String. A single RelativeDistinguishedName is handled the same way. An ORAddress is written as the textual form from RFC 2156, quoted like an IA5String.

Types such as unrestricted CHARACTER STRING, EMBEDDED PDV, EXTERNAL and INSTANCE OF are encoded as the sequence types that the ASN.1 standards define for them.

GSER also has its own object identifier, { 1 2 36 79672281 0 0 }, which could be used to name it as the transfer syntax of a value inside an EMBEDDED PDV.
sections.eli5: Some things, like a full address in a directory, already had a favorite way to be written as text. GSER just keeps using that way.

sections.title: Not Canonical, Not for Signatures
sections.content:
GSER does not define a canonical encoding. Turning a GSER value into another encoding such as BER and back will not necessarily give the same GSER bytes. GSER also cannot always rebuild the exact octets of TeletexString, VideotexString, GraphicString or GeneralString values, so a trip from DER to GSER and back to DER may not match the original.

So GSER MUST NOT be used where a canonical encoding is needed, or to re-encode values whose original binary encoding must be recoverable. Digital signature verification is the example given, and protocols ought to use DER or a DER-reversible encoding there. In security-sensitive fields, especially those that grant or deny access, comparisons MUST be made on the underlying abstract value, whatever the encoding.
sections.eli5: If you translate a message into plain words and back, it might not come out letter for letter the same. That is fine for reading but not for something that has to match exactly, like a signature.

viz.caption: HOW SIMPLE ASN.1 TYPES LOOK IN GSER

Hex digits in single quotes followed by H
Binary digits followed by B, hex followed by H, or a list of named bits
